chapters.screen: Ridge Regression. Keep all twelve powers of income, but charge the model for large weights. Watch the penalty α grow: the wiggly curve calms down, the weights shrink smoothly, and validation finds the sweet spot.
chapters.spoken: Ridge Regression. Keep all twelve powers of income, but charge the model for large weights. Watch the penalty alpha grow: the wiggly curve calms down, the weights shrink smoothly, and validation finds the sweet spot.

chapters.screen: Each dot is one California district: median income (x) and median house value (y). This lesson is trained on just 30 districts, one from each income band, so over-fitting is easy to see; 4,128 other districts judge it.
chapters.spoken: Each dot is one California district: median income and median house value. This lesson is trained on just 30 districts, one from each income band, so over-fitting is easy to see; 4,128 other districts judge it.

chapters.screen: Almost no penalty (α = 1.0e-5): the degree-12 curve bends to chase the 30 training districts.
chapters.spoken: Almost no penalty (alpha equals 10 to the minus 5): the degree-12 curve bends to chase the 30 training districts.

chapters.screen: Each frame refits with a stronger penalty. Ridge minimises squared error + α × (sum of squared weights), so every weight shrinks but never quite reaches zero.
chapters.spoken: Each frame refits with a stronger penalty. Ridge minimises squared error plus alpha times (sum of squared weights), so every weight shrinks but never quite reaches zero.

chapters.screen: Validation chose α = 4.6e-1: train RMSE $59k, validation $84k. Too much penalty flattens the curve towards the average.
chapters.spoken: Validation chose alpha equals 0.46: train root mean squared error 59 thousand dollars, validation 84 thousand dollars. Too much penalty flattens the curve towards the average.

chapters.screen: The tamed polynomial prices an unseen district. Small weights mean small pushes, so no single power of income can swing the price wildly.
chapters.spoken: The tamed polynomial prices an unseen district. Small weights mean small pushes, so no single power of income can swing the price wildly.

chapters.screen: Final exam: the trained model prices all 4,128 test districts it has never seen, a batch at a time. The map shows where it misses: blue = worth more than predicted.
chapters.spoken: Final exam: the trained model prices all 4,128 test districts it has never seen, a batch at a time. The map shows where it misses: blue means worth more than predicted.

chapters.screen: Ridge fits a degree-12 polynomial of both inputs; the penalty α, chosen on validation, decides how smooth the sheet stays. Same algorithm, now given house age as well as income; height is its predicted price.
chapters.spoken: Ridge fits a degree-12 polynomial of both inputs; the penalty alpha, chosen on validation, decides how smooth the sheet stays. Same algorithm, now given house age as well as income; height is its predicted price.

chapters.screen: Seven more inputs cut the typical error from $85k to $75k.
chapters.spoken: Seven more inputs cut the typical error from 85 thousand dollars to 75 thousand dollars.

chapters.screen: Ridge trades a little training error for a smoother curve: shrinking every weight reduces over-fitting without removing any feature. Limitation: α must be tuned on held-out data, and Ridge never sets a weight to exactly zero, so it cannot tell you which terms are unnecessary.
chapters.spoken: Ridge trades a little training error for a smoother curve: shrinking every weight reduces over-fitting without removing any feature. Limitation: alpha must be tuned on held-out data, and Ridge never sets a weight to exactly zero, so it cannot tell you which terms are unnecessary.
